intro: Sleeping well on a mountain is part of climbing it. A good shelter keeps you dry, out of the wind and rested enough to make good decisions the next day.

items.name: Mountaineering tent
items.text: A strong, low tent built to take wind and snow loading. Double-wall tents are warmer and have less condensation. Single-wall tents are lighter.
tips: Pitch with the narrow end into the wind.
Dig the platform flat and build snow walls on the windward side.
Keep the vents open even if it is cold, to limit condensation.

items.name: Bivouac
items.text: Sleeping out with only a bivy bag, a sleeping bag and what you carry. Most often an emergency, sometimes a plan.
tips: Find a ledge out of rockfall and wind.
Keep your boots and gloves inside the bag so they do not freeze.
Eat and drink before you settle in.

items.name: Snow cave
items.text: Dug into a deep, stable snow drift. Surprisingly warm and quiet, with temperatures near freezing even when it is far colder outside.
tips: Dig a sleeping platform higher than the entrance so cold air stays below.
Make a ventilation hole in the roof and keep the entrance clear.
Keep your shovel inside with you.

items.name: Igloo and quinzhee
items.text: An igloo is cut from blocks of firm snow. A quinzhee is a mound of snow that has set and been hollowed out. Both are slow to build but make a solid winter shelter.
tips: Allow a few hours to build.
Wait for a quinzhee mound to harden before digging.

items.name: Mountain huts and refuges
items.text: The Alps have a network of staffed huts, which makes multi-day trips possible without carrying a tent. The Capanna Regina Margherita, at 4,554 m on the Italian-Swiss border, is the highest hut in Europe.
tips: Bring a sleeping bag liner, earplugs and a head torch.
Leave early; most climbers set off before dawn.

items.name: Base camp and high camps
items.text: On big expeditions, Base Camp is a small town of tents with kitchen, dining and communications. Higher camps are small and basic, used only for a night or two.
tips: Camp away from avalanche paths and icefall.
Treat waste properly. Many camps now require you to carry it down.
Tie down everything; a high-camp wind can take a tent.

checklist: Pick a site that is flat, out of the wind and away from avalanche runouts, rockfall and cornices.
Anchor every guy line with snow stakes, buried axes or rocks.
Ventilate any enclosed shelter. Carbon monoxide from a stove can kill.
Never cook inside a closed tent without ventilation, and never sleep with a stove burning.
Melt snow for water before you rest. Dehydration slows recovery.
